name: Block Header
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Fingerprint That Anchors a Block
lesson.summary: The block header is the compact metadata section of a block that includes the previous block's hash, a timestamp, and a summary of the block's transactions, and it is the header, not the raw transaction data, that actually links one block to the next.
lesson.body:
The previous section split a block into a header and a body and noted that the header is smaller but structurally more important. This section looks closely at why. When people say a block is "linked" to the block before it by a cryptographic hash, what is actually being hashed and referenced is the previous block's header, not its entire body of transactions. The header, in other words, is the part of a block doing the actual chain forming work described back in the blockchain definition section.

A typical block header contains several distinct fields, and each does a specific job. The previous block hash is the cryptographic fingerprint of the prior header, and it is this field that makes the structure a chain rather than a loose pile of blocks. A timestamp records roughly when the block was created, useful for ordering and for consensus rules that check whether a block's claimed time is plausible. A Merkle root is a single hash that summarizes every transaction in the block's body, built by repeatedly hashing pairs of transactions together until only one hash remains at the top of the tree. And depending on the consensus mechanism, there may be a nonce or similar field, a number miners adjust and re-hash against in proof of work systems while searching for a header hash that meets the network's difficulty target.

This connects directly to cryptographic hashing covered earlier in this course: a hash function takes input of any size and produces a fixed size, seemingly random output, and even a tiny change to the input produces a completely different output. The header's own hash, computed by hashing the header fields together, therefore changes entirely if the previous block hash field changes, if the Merkle root changes because a single transaction in the body was altered, or if the nonce changes. This is exactly the mechanism that gives blockchains their tamper evidence: you cannot alter a transaction in a block's body without changing the Merkle root, which changes the header, which changes the header's hash, which breaks the reference the next block relies on.

The Merkle root deserves a concrete illustration, because it is doing more work than it might look like. Suppose a block contains four transactions, A, B, C, and D. Rather than the header storing all four transactions directly, the system hashes A and B together to get one value, hashes C and D together to get another, then hashes those two values together to get the single Merkle root stored in the header. To prove that transaction C is included in the block, you do not need the whole block body, you only need transaction C, the hash of D, and the combined hash of A and B, a small handful of values that let anyone recompute the Merkle root and check it matches the header. This is precisely how lightweight clients can verify a specific transaction was included in a block without downloading every transaction in it.

The upshot is that the header is a compact commitment to everything in the block, both its own place in the chain and the full contents of its body, without needing to carry that full content along with it. Everything downstream in this course that talks about verifying a chain quickly, syncing a lightweight client, or proving a transaction happened, ultimately relies on this small, fixed structure piece of metadata doing an outsized amount of cryptographic work.
